purpose: Teach the production infrastructure and operating disciplines behind model, language-model, and agent applications, including cloud foundations, environments, pipelines, artifacts, deployment, observability, cost, resilience, incidents, recovery, and exit.
staffSummary: Build M43 around one consequential utility situation and one decision: Design the smallest supportable architecture and operating pipeline for a bounded utility application, assign every responsibility, and define release, observation, incident, rollback, cost, support, and exit evidence. The learner must leave with a usable AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record, not a collection of definitions.
openingSituation: A prototype works on one laptop, then fails in production because configuration, secrets, dependencies, traffic, logs, backups, updates, and ownership were never designed.
learnerDecision: Design the smallest supportable architecture and operating pipeline for a bounded utility application, assign every responsibility, and define release, observation, incident, rollback, cost, support, and exit evidence.
analogy: A pump is only one part of a pump station. Power, controls, housing, access, maintenance, alarms, and backup make it an operating system.
learnerOutcomes: Explain The Infrastructure: Containers, Docker, DigitalOcean, Deployment, Scaling Laws in plain English and connect it to a real water, wastewater, stormwater, or One Water decision.

Distinguish development, test, production, container, compute, storage, network, identity, secret, artifact, pipeline, continuous integration, delivery, deployment, observability, drift, incident, scaling, recovery, and exit without using one term to hide several different jobs.
Analyze the module situation, identify missing evidence, and name the professional consequence of a weak decision.
Compare how the same question changes across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, administration, engineering, finance, technology, and public leadership.

Evaluate sources, assumptions, limitations, permissions, and human authority using this boundary: Keep services, prices, limits, model versions, platform features, and scaling claims dated. Do not publish credentials or facility-sensitive architecture, skip security review, or represent a classroom deployment as a supported production service.
Create a usable AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record with evidence, roles, limits, review steps, and the next accountable action.
Defend the recommendation to Foundation, Practitioner, and Leader audiences while keeping disagreement and uncertainty visible.
curriculumOutcomes: Give The Infrastructure: Containers, Docker, DigitalOcean, Deployment, Scaling Laws one clear learning job inside Building AI Systems.
Connect the module to a consequential decision and the AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record.
Preserve current content, proposals, enhancements, and contributor records by stable identifier.
Separate verified evidence, Hardeep positions, expert interpretation, instructional scenarios, and unresolved questions.
Create an explicit bridge to the preceding and following modules without duplicating their work.
marketingOutcomes: Describe the practical value as helping a learner make and explain this decision: Design the smallest supportable architecture and operating pipeline for a bounded utility application, assign every responsibility, and define release, observation, incident, rollback, cost, support, and exit evidence.
Name the AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record as the visible result of the module.
Do not promise savings, compliance, certification, safety, performance, implementation success, or career outcomes without separately approved evidence.
requiredWorkProduct: AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record
definitionOfDone: The learner explains the core distinctions, completes the required evidence and decision activities, passes distributed checks, saves a complete AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record, and names the next accountable action.
scopeBoundary: Keep services, prices, limits, model versions, platform features, and scaling claims dated. Do not publish credentials or facility-sensitive architecture, skip security review, or represent a classroom deployment as a supported production service.
researchQuestions: What must an intelligent newcomer understand about The Infrastructure: Containers, Docker, DigitalOcean, Deployment, Scaling Laws before using it in utility work?

Which sources can support the distinctions among development, test, production, container, compute, storage, network, identity, secret, artifact, pipeline, continuous integration, delivery, deployment, observability, drift, incident, scaling, recovery, and exit?

What evidence would allow a practitioner to make this decision: Design the smallest supportable architecture and operating pipeline for a bounded utility application, assign every responsibility, and define release, observation, incident, rollback, cost, support, and exit evidence.
Which failure modes, counterexamples, and edge conditions could make the AI deployment, operations, and release architecture record misleading?
How does the question change across drinking water, wastewater, stormwater, reuse, finance, engineering, administration, technology, and public accountability?
Which actions require qualified operator, engineer, water-quality, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, procurement, records, finance, accessibility, or executive review?

Which claims remain outside the module boundary: Keep services, prices, limits, model versions, platform features, and scaling claims dated. Do not publish credentials or facility-sensitive architecture, skip security review, or represent a classroom deployment as a supported production service.

acceptedExpansions.title: Machine Learning Operations pipelines and reproducibility
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Teach the operating pipeline that moves data, code, model artifacts, tests, approvals, and monitoring through controlled environments. The learner must be able to reproduce a release and recover from a failed one.
acceptedExpansions.description: Teach the operating pipeline that moves data, code, model artifacts, tests, approvals, and monitoring through controlled environments. The learner must be able to reproduce a release and recover from a failed one.
learningObjectives: Explain Machine Learning Operations in plain English as the controlled path from model work to supported operation.
Map data, code, experiment, model, test, environment, release, monitoring, and rollback dependencies.
Distinguish version control, experiment tracking, artifact storage, continuous integration, continuous delivery, and deployment.
Diagnose a reproducibility failure and identify the missing version, dependency, data, or configuration evidence.
Create a vendor-neutral Machine Learning Operations pipeline and release record.
acceptedExpansions.workProduct: Machine Learning Operations pipeline and release record
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: Use synthetic or approved data. Do not represent a classroom pipeline as a supported production service or a validated predictive model.

subtopics.title: Data, code, model, configuration, and environment versions
Release approval, deployment strategies, and rollback
Performance degradation, data drift, model drift, and correction

acceptedExpansions.title: Large Language Model Operations and agent operations
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Unify prompt, context, retrieval, tools, models, evaluations, traces, cost, incidents, and human review as one operating discipline for language-model and agent systems.
acceptedExpansions.description: Unify prompt, context, retrieval, tools, models, evaluations, traces, cost, incidents, and human review as one operating discipline for language-model and agent systems.
learningObjectives: Explain how Large Language Model Operations differs from ordinary model deployment and ordinary software operation.
Version prompts, system instructions, retrieval sources, tools, permissions, evaluations, and model choices as operating dependencies.
Inspect a trace and separate model, source, tool, permission, orchestration, and human-review failures.
Define operating measures for quality, groundedness, refusal, tool correctness, latency, cost, and review effort.
Create an agent operations record with monitoring, incident, rollback, and human-escalation rules.
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: A trace shows what the system recorded. It does not prove completeness, correctness, legal sufficiency, or professional judgment.

subtopics.title: Prompt, context, retrieval, model, tool, and policy versions
Offline evaluation, regression testing, and online observation
Traces, tool calls, state transitions, and human review
Latency, token use, cost limits, rate limits, and capacity
Agent incidents, containment, retry limits, escalation, and rollback
Ownership, service levels, support, and retirement

acceptedExpansions.title: Cloud foundations and managed AI platforms
acceptedExpansions.recommendation: Teach a vendor-neutral cloud foundation before a learner enters an Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, or other platform lab. Every managed service still has identity, data, logging, cost, support, and exit responsibilities.
acceptedExpansions.description: Teach a vendor-neutral cloud foundation before a learner enters an Azure, Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, or other platform lab. Every managed service still has identity, data, logging, cost, support, and exit responsibilities.
learningObjectives: Explain cloud region, network, compute, storage, identity, secret, log, managed model endpoint, and service responsibility in plain English.
Map data and request flow across a minimum supportable hosted artificial intelligence application.
Compare managed, self-hosted, local, and hybrid patterns for capability, control, privacy, cost, support, and exit.
Identify identity, permission, secret, network, logging, backup, cost, resilience, and vendor-dependency requirements.
Create a vendor-neutral cloud AI responsibility and exit map.
acceptedExpansions.workProduct: cloud AI responsibility and exit map
acceptedExpansions.evidenceBoundary: Named platforms are dated examples. A managed service does not remove the utility's responsibility for data, access, evaluation, contract, cost, records, or accountable use.
